page: Amazon Web Services i2.4xlarge is a storage-optimized second-generation instance designed for workloads requiring high local storage capacity and memory. It features 16 vCPUs powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 processor running at 2.5 GHz, with 8 physical cores and 2 threads per core under the Xen hypervisor. The instance is equipped with 122.0 GB of system memory, providing 7.62 GB per core. For local storage, it includes 3200 GB of NVMe SSD capacity. Network connectivity is supported by a baseline bandwidth of 2 Gbps, and there are no complimentary public IPv4 addresses included.

Benchmark data indicates average performance across several core compute and memory metrics, alongside some notable limitations. The Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 processor achieves average ratings in stress-ng single-core (1623.49) and multi-core (14125.68) tests, as well as in PassMark CPU (16683.51) and database operations (6516.2). However, single-core processing capabilities are limited, as shown by poor ratings in Geekbench single-core (532.0) and text processing (1080.0). Memory bandwidth is highly asymmetric; while cached small-block read operations reach an average of 588.91 GB/sec, large-block write bandwidth is weak at 18.74 GB/sec. Similarly, single-threaded compression and decompression tasks show weak to poor performance, with bzip3 single-threaded decompression scoring in the bottom 10% at 7.37 GB/sec.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the i2.4xlarge offers a high density of local NVMe SSD storage and memory relative to its compute resources, making it a viable option for legacy storage-heavy workloads. However, its older architecture results in lower performance-per-resource ratios for modern tasks like machine learning, where LLM inference speeds for a 7B model are weak (7.2 tokens/sec for text generation). This instance is best suited for relational databases, NoSQL databases, transactional data stores, and static web serving, where its 14.27 GB/sec static web serving throughput and 6.04 million operations per second in Redis SET benchmarks can be leveraged.
